_about: Learner-friendly entries shown before WordNet: grammar words that WordNet does not cover (or covers only with rare meanings), and modern words newer than WordNet 3.0. Format: word -> [[part of speech, definition, example], ...]. Parts of speech noun/verb/adjective/adverb also match inflected forms (apps -> app).
a: used before a singular noun when you do not say which one, or when it is mentioned for the first time (use "an" before a vowel sound)
I saw a dog in the park.
an: the form of "a" used before a vowel sound
She ate an apple and an orange.
the: used before a noun when it is clear which thing or person you mean
i: the person who is speaking or writing
myself: used when the person speaking is also the object, or for emphasis
you: the person or people that someone is speaking or writing to
yourself: used when "you" (one person) is also the object, or for emphasis
yourselves: used when "you" (more than one person) is also the object
he: a man, boy or male animal already mentioned
Tom is late because he missed the bus.
himself: used when "he" is also the object, or for emphasis
she: a woman, girl or female animal already mentioned
Anna is tired because she worked late.
herself: used when "she" is also the object, or for emphasis
it: a thing, animal or situation already mentioned; also used as an empty subject
It is raining. I like this film; it is funny.
its: belonging to it (no apostrophe; "it's" means "it is")
itself: used when "it" is also the object, or for emphasis
we: the speaker and one or more other people
We are going to the beach.
ourselves: used when "we" is also the object, or for emphasis
they: people or things already mentioned; also used for one person whose gender is not known
My parents say they are proud.
themselves: used when "they" is also the object, or for emphasis
oneself: used when "one" (people in general) is also the object
It is important to look after oneself.
who: used to ask which person; also joins information about a person
Who is that? The man who lives next door is a doctor.
whom: To whom should I send the letter?
whose: belonging to which person; also joins information about who something belongs to
Whose bag is this? The girl whose bike was stolen called the police.
which: used to ask about one of a limited group; also joins extra information about a thing
Which colour do you want? The book, which is new, is very good.
what: used to ask for information about something; also "the thing that"
What is your name? I know what you mean.
that: used for a person or thing further away or already mentioned
used to introduce a clause, especially after verbs like say, think and know
She said that she was tired.
used to join information about a person or thing
The film that we saw was great.
this: used for a person or thing near you or being talked about now
something: a thing that is not known or not named
There is something in my shoe.
anything: any thing at all (often in questions and negatives)
nothing: There is nothing in the box.
someone: a person who is not known or not named
others: Some students walk to school; others take the bus.
some: an amount or number of something, without saying exactly how much or many
any: some, or one of many, often in questions and negatives
every: all the people or things in a group, one by one
I walk to school every day.
each: every one of two or more things, seen separately
both: the two people or things together
either: one or the other of two
You can sit on either side.
neither: not one and not the other of two
all: the whole number or amount of something
no: used to give a negative answer
many: a large number of (used with countable nouns)
much: a large amount of (used with uncountable nouns, often in questions and negatives)
few: a small number of; "a few" means some
Few people came. I have a few friends here.
most: the largest number or amount; nearly all
per: The tickets cost five dollars per person.
to: in the direction of; also used before a verb to make the infinitive
We went to the market. I want to learn English.
of: belonging to, part of, or containing
a cup of tea, the end of the film
for: intended for someone; for a period of time; for a purpose
This gift is for you. I waited for two hours.
with: I live with my parents. Cut it with a knife.
from: showing where someone or something starts or comes from
into: moving to the inside of something; changing to
onto: moving to a position on top of something
The cat jumped onto the table.
in: inside a place or thing; during a period of time
The keys are in my bag. I was born in 2010.
on: touching the top surface of something; on a day or date
The book is on the table. See you on Monday.
at: showing an exact place or time
Meet me at the station at six o'clock.
by: near; showing who did something; using a means of transport
She sat by the window. The book was written by her. We went by bus.
during: all through, or at some point in, a period of time
until: The shop is open until nine.
since: from a time in the past until now
Since it was raining, we stayed home.
among: in the middle of, or as part of, a group
She was among the best students.
against: Many people are against the plan.
towards: in the direction of; in relation to
despite: We went out despite the rain.
amid: in the middle of, or during
The decision came amid strong criticism.
via: We flew to London via Dubai.
within: inside; before the end of a period of time
like: She looks like her mother. I enjoy sports like football.
unlike: Unlike his brother, he is very quiet.
and: joins words or ideas that go together
but: joins two ideas that are different or opposite
It was cold, but we went out.
or: Would you like tea or coffee?
nor: and not (used after "neither" or a negative)
so: I was tired, so I went to bed.
because: I stayed home because I was ill.
if: If it rains, we will stay inside.
unless: You will be late unless you hurry.
whether: used to talk about a choice between possibilities
I don't know whether to go or stay.
when: at the time that; also used to ask about time
Call me when you arrive. When is your birthday?
whenever: every time that; at any time
where: in or to which place; also used to ask about place
Where do you live? This is the house where I grew up.
how: in what way; to what degree
How do you make this? How old are you?
although: used to introduce something that makes the main idea surprising
Although it was late, she kept working.
though: Though he was tired, he finished the race.
whereas: used to compare two facts and show how they are different
I like tea, whereas my sister prefers coffee.
while: during the time that; also used to contrast two ideas
She called while I was cooking.
whereby: a system whereby students choose their own subjects
albeit: It was a success, albeit a small one.
lest: a formal word meaning "in order to prevent something"
They spoke quietly lest anyone hear them.
can: to be able to; to be allowed to
I can swim. You can go now.
could: the past of "can"; also used for possibility and polite requests
I could read when I was four. Could you help me?
will: used to talk about the future, and for promises and offers
would: used for imagined situations, polite requests, and as the past of "will"
I would buy a house if I were rich. Would you like some tea?
shall: used with I and we for offers and suggestions; a formal form of "will"
should: used to give advice or say what is right
may: used for possibility, or to ask for or give permission
It may rain later. May I come in?
might: used to say something is possible but not certain
We might go to the beach tomorrow.
must: used to say something is necessary, or to say you are sure
You must wear a seatbelt. She must be tired.
ought: You ought to see a doctor.
app: a computer program, especially one you download onto a phone
I use an app to learn English.
smartphone: a mobile phone that can connect to the internet and run apps
selfie: a photo you take of yourself, usually with a phone
We took a selfie at the beach.
inbox: the place where your new emails or messages arrive
I have fifty emails in my inbox.
offline: You can read the book offline.
chatbot: a computer program that you can have a written or spoken conversation with
The website has a chatbot to answer questions.
dataset: a collection of data, usually stored on a computer
The researchers studied a large dataset.
influencer: a person who is paid by companies to show or talk about products on social media
The influencer has a million followers.
autoplay: a feature that starts the next video or song automatically
Turn off autoplay to stop watching.
repost: to share something on social media that someone else has posted
audiobook: a recording of a book being read aloud
I listen to audiobooks on the bus.
podcaster: a person who makes podcasts (audio programmes you can download or stream)
The podcaster interviews a scientist every week.
policymaker: a person, often in government, who decides on plans and rules
Policymakers must act on climate change.
burnout: a state of being extremely tired and unable to work because of too much work or stress
Long hours can lead to burnout.
heatwave: a period of unusually hot weather
The heatwave lasted for two weeks.
microplastic: a very small piece of plastic, often too small to see, that pollutes water and soil
Microplastics have been found in the ocean.
greenwashing: trying to make a company or product seem better for the environment than it really is
Critics accused the company of greenwashing.
groundwater: water that is held under the ground in soil and rocks
The village gets its water from groundwater.
overfishing: catching so many fish that there are not enough left to breed
Overfishing has reduced the number of cod.
overgrazing: letting animals eat so much grass that the land is damaged
Overgrazing turned the field to dust.
rewild: to return land to a natural state, often by bringing back wild animals and plants
The farmers decided to rewild part of the valley.
rewilding: the process of returning land to a natural state
Rewilding projects have brought back wolves.
megafauna: large animals, such as mammoths, elephants and bison
Many megafauna died out at the end of the ice age.
voluntourism: travelling to another country to do volunteer work as part of a holiday
storytelling: Storytelling is an important part of the culture.
soundscape: all the sounds you can hear in a particular place
the soundscape of a busy city
timescale: the amount of time something takes or needs
The project has a long timescale.
helpline: a telephone service where people can get advice or help
Call the helpline if you need support.
noticeboard: a board on a wall where notices are put up
The timetable is on the noticeboard.
letterbox: a hole in a door where letters are delivered
The postman put the card through the letterbox.
sandcastle: a model of a castle made of sand on a beach
sweaty: My shirt was sweaty after the run.
greyscale: a range of shades from black to white, with no colour
treatable: able to be cured or treated by doctors
The disease is treatable if found early.
testable: able to be checked by a test or experiment
nuanced: showing small but important differences in meaning or opinion
complicit: involved with others in doing something wrong
They were complicit in the crime.
unsustainable: not able to continue at the same level or rate, often because it damages the environment
Our use of plastic is unsustainable.
sustainably: in a way that does not damage the environment and can continue for a long time
showcase: to show the best qualities of something
remastered: (of a recording) improved with new technology
a remastered version of the album
craftspeople: people who make things skilfully by hand
Local craftspeople sell their work at the market.
bioethicist: an expert in the moral questions raised by medicine and biology
nocebo: a harmless treatment that makes someone feel worse because they expect bad effects
Warning patients about side effects can cause a nocebo effect.
preregistration: publishing a study's plan before collecting data, so the results cannot be changed to fit
Preregistration helps to prevent misleading results.
prebunking: warning people about false information before they see it, so they are less likely to believe it
Prebunking can reduce the spread of fake news.
credentialism: relying too much on qualifications such as degrees when judging people
Critics say credentialism shuts out talented people.
maximiser: a person who always tries to make the best possible choice
Maximisers often feel less satisfied with their choices.
satisficer: a person who accepts the first choice that is good enough
Satisficers tend to be happier with their decisions.
compatibilist: a person who believes that free will is possible even if all events have causes
Compatibilists argue that we can still be responsible.
polycentric: having many centres of control or power
aestheticise: to present something as beautiful or artistic, often ignoring its unpleasant side
birdwatcher: a person who watches wild birds as a hobby
Birdwatchers counted the birds in the park.
conflation: treating two different ideas or things as if they were the same
a conflation of wealth and happiness
foreignise: (in translation) to keep the foreign feel of the original text instead of making it sound natural in the new language
Some translators prefer to foreignise the text.
foreignising: a way of translating that keeps the foreign feel of the original text
Foreignising makes the reader aware they are reading a translation.
incommensurability: the state of having no common standard, so that two things cannot be fairly compared
the incommensurability of the two theories
ineliminable: impossible to remove or get rid of
mori: used in "memento mori": an object or image that reminds people that they will die
The skull in the painting is a memento mori.
nepotistic: giving jobs or advantages to your own family or friends unfairly
radiometric: measuring the age of rocks or objects from the rate at which radioactive elements decay
snorkeller: a person who swims under the surface of the water using a snorkel (a tube for breathing)
The reef is popular with snorkellers.
stratigraphic: relating to the layers of rock in the ground and what they show about the past
untranslatability: the quality of being impossible to translate exactly into another language
untranslatable: a word or phrase that cannot be translated exactly into another language
pho: a Vietnamese soup made with rice noodles and beef or chicken
hoc: used in "ad hoc": made or done only for a particular purpose, not planned
versa: used in "vice versa": the other way round
Cats chase dogs and vice versa.
lunchbox: a box that you carry your lunch in, for example to school
My lunchbox has a sandwich and an apple in it.
goodnight: something you say to someone before they go to bed or when you leave in the evening
Goodnight, Mum! See you in the morning.
headteacher: the teacher who is in charge of a school
The headteacher gave prizes to the winners.
keyring: a ring that you keep your keys on, often with a small toy or picture
I bought a panda keyring at the zoo.
mooncake: a round sweet cake eaten at the Mid-Autumn Festival
We ate mooncakes and looked at the full moon.
